title: Unit aliases
text:
Unit aliases

PyAnsys Units supports unit aliases, allowing you to use shorthand or
alternative names for units. For example, you can write deg instead of
degree, meter instead of m, or newton instead of N.

Aliases resolve transparently to their canonical unit names during parsing,
so they work everywhere a unit string is accepted: Unit(), Quantity(),
compound unit strings, and conversions.

text:

title: Unit aliases > Registering custom aliases
text:
Registering custom aliases

You can register your own aliases at runtime using the
UnitRegistry.register_alias() method:

The method validates that:

The alias does not shadow an existing base unit, derived unit, or alias
(raises AliasAlreadyRegistered).

The canonical target is a configured unit or an existing alias
(raises ValueError).

Neither argument is empty (raises ValueError).

Aliases can also point to other aliases. The resolution follows the chain
transitively until a canonical unit is reached:

Aliases registered programmatically via register_alias() are added to the
global alias table. They take effect immediately for all subsequent
Unit() and Quantity() calls in the same process. They are not
persisted across sessions.

title: Unit aliases > Aliases for custom registered units
text:
Aliases for custom registered units

The aliases argument on UnitRegistry.register_unit() is a different,
more narrowly scoped mechanism: it adds alternative names for a single custom
unit on that registry instance only. Unlike register_alias(), it does
not modify the global alias table and has no effect on Unit() or on other
registries.

title: Unit registry
text:
Unit registry



class ansys.units.unit_registry.UnitRegistry(config: str = 'cfg.yaml', other: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, Any]] = {}, custom_units: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]] | None = None, custom_units_file: str | None = None)

Bases: object

A representation of valid Unit instances.

All base and derived units loaded from the configuration file, cfg.yaml,
on package initialization are provided by default.

Parameters

config: str, optional

Path of a YAML configuration file, which can be a custom file, and
defaults to the provided file, cfg.yaml. Custom configuration files
must match the format of the default configuration file.

other: dict, optional

Dictionary for additional units (uses config file format).

custom_units

python:list of python:dict, optional

List of custom units to register during construction. Each dict must
have keys "unit", "composition", and "factor" matching
the register_unit() signature. An optional "aliases" key
(a list of strings) is also supported.

custom_units_file

python:str, optional

Path to a YAML file previously produced by
export_custom_units(). Entries are loaded and registered the
same way as custom_units, and the two can be combined.

Examples

>>> from ansys.units import UnitRegistry, Unit
>>> ureg = UnitRegistry()
>>> assert ureg.kg == Unit(units="kg")
>>> fps = Unit("ft s^-1")
>>> ureg.foot_per_sec = fps

Register custom units at construction:

>>> ur = UnitRegistry(custom_units=[
...     {"unit": "micron", "composition": "m", "factor": 1e-6},
...     {"unit": "inch", "composition": "m", "factor": 0.0254},
...     {"unit": "furlong", "composition": "m", "factor": 201.168,
...      "aliases": ["furlongs"]},
... ])
>>> q = ur.Quantity(10, "micron")



Quantity(value: float | _ArrayInput, units: str | Unit) -> Quantity

Create a Quantity using this registry’s units.

This method allows creating quantities with instance-registered units
using string names.

Parameters

value

python:int, python:float, or python:sequence

The numeric value.

units

python:str or Unit

The unit name (looked up in this registry) or a Unit object.

Returns

Quantity

The created quantity.

Examples

>>> ur = UnitRegistry()
>>> ur.register_unit(unit="micron", composition="m", factor=1e-6)
>>> q = ur.Quantity(1, "micron")
>>> print(q)
1.0 micron



export_custom_units(path: str, *, overwrite: bool = False) -> None

Export this registry’s runtime-registered custom units to a YAML file.

Only units registered via register_unit() (directly, or through
the custom_units/custom_units_file constructor parameters) are
exported. Built-in units are never included. The resulting file can be
reloaded with load_custom_units() or passed directly as
custom_units_file to a new UnitRegistry.

Parameters

path

python:str

Destination file path.

overwrite

bool, optional

Whether to overwrite path if it already exists. Default is
False.

Raises

ValueError

If this registry has no custom registered units to export.

FileExistsError

If path already exists and overwrite is False.

Examples

>>> from ansys.units.common import m
>>> ur = UnitRegistry()
>>> ur.register_unit("furlong", 201.168 * m, aliases=["furlongs"])
>>> ur.export_custom_units("units.yaml")
>>> ur2 = UnitRegistry(custom_units_file="units.yaml")
>>> ur2.furlong is ur2.furlongs
True



get_unit(name: str) -> Unit

Look up a unit by name from this registry.

Checks instance-registered units first, then falls back to built-in
units and compound unit strings. This allows string-based lookup of
custom registered units as well as standard unit expressions.

Parameters

name

python:str

The unit name or compound unit string to look up (e.g., “micron”,
“m”, “kg mol^-1”).

Returns

Unit

The unit object.

Raises

AttributeError

If the unit is not found in this registry or cannot be parsed.



register_alias(alias: str, canonical: str) -> None

Register a new alias for an existing unit.

The alias is added to the global alias table so that it can be used
anywhere a unit string is accepted (Unit(), Quantity(), etc.).

Parameters

alias

python:str

The alias name (e.g., "deg").

canonical

python:str

The canonical unit name the alias resolves to
(e.g., "degree"). Must be a configured base or derived unit,
or an existing alias.

Raises

AliasAlreadyRegistered

If alias is already registered as a unit or alias.

ValueError

If canonical is not a known unit or alias.



register_unit(unit: str, definition: Unit | Quantity[Any], *, aliases: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> Unit

register_unit(*, unit: str, composition: str, factor: float, aliases: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> Unit

Register a new derived unit on this UnitRegistry instance.

This is instance-scoped: it affects only this registry and does not
mutate global state or other registries. The registered unit can be
accessed as an attribute (e.g., ur.micron) or via
get_unit() for string-based lookup.

This method supports two equivalent calling conventions: an
object-based form that accepts a Unit or Quantity definition,
and a composition/factor form.

Parameters

unit: str

The symbol/name of the new unit (e.g., “micron”).

definition: Unit or Quantity, optional

An object-based definition of the new unit, for example
201.168 * m (a Quantity) or a bare Unit instance
(treated as a factor of 1). Mutually exclusive with
composition/factor.

composition: str, optional

A valid unit composition using existing configured units (e.g., “m”).
Must be provided together with factor. Mutually exclusive with
definition.

factor: float, optional

Scale factor that relates the composition to this unit. Must be
provided together with composition. Mutually exclusive with
definition.

aliases: sequence of str, optional

Additional names that resolve to the same registered unit on this
instance (e.g., ["furlongs"]).

Returns

Unit

The registered unit attached on this instance.

Raises

UnitNameAlreadyRegistered

If unit (or one of aliases) is a built-in unit name, or
already exists on this instance with a different effective
definition (dimensions, SI scaling factor, or SI offset).
Re-registering the same name with an equivalent definition is a
no-op that returns the existing unit.

ValueError

If unit or an alias is empty, factor is not finite, or
both/neither of definition and composition/factor are
given.

Notes

The duplicate-name check compares effective definitions (dimensions,
SI scaling factor, and SI offset). Re-registering the same name with
an equivalent definition is idempotent. Built-in unit names can never
be overridden, even with an equivalent definition. The check does not
detect equivalent definitions registered under a different name.

Examples

>>> ur = UnitRegistry()
>>> ur.register_unit(unit="micron", composition="m", factor=1e-6)
>>> q = ur.Quantity(1, "micron")  # Use registry's Quantity method

Object-based form, with an alias:

>>> from ansys.units.common import m
>>> ur.register_unit("furlong", 201.168 * m, aliases=["furlongs"])
>>> ur.furlong == ur.furlongs
True



ansys.units.unit_registry.load_custom_units(path: str) -> list[dict[str, Any]]

Load custom unit definitions from a file written by export_custom_units.

Parameters

path

python:str

Path to a YAML file previously produced by
UnitRegistry.export_custom_units().

Returns

python:list of python:dict

A list of custom unit definitions, suitable for passing directly as
the custom_units constructor parameter of UnitRegistry.

Examples

>>> ur.export_custom_units("units.yaml")
>>> custom_units = load_custom_units("units.yaml")
>>> ur2 = UnitRegistry(custom_units=custom_units)



exception ansys.units.unit_registry.UnitNameAlreadyRegistered(name: str)

Bases: ValueError

Raised when a unit name conflicts with an existing name.

This is raised when unit (or an alias) is a built-in unit name, or when it is
already registered on the instance with a different effective definition
(dimensions, SI scaling factor, or SI offset). Re-registering the same name with an
equivalent definition is a no-op and does not raise. Units with different names but
equivalent definitions (same composition and factor) are also not detected as
conflicts.



exception ansys.units.unit_registry.AliasAlreadyRegistered(name: str)

Bases: ValueError

Raised when an alias conflicts with an existing unit or alias.

Bases: ValueError

Raised when a unit name conflicts with an existing name.

This is raised when unit (or an alias) is a built-in unit name, or when it is
already registered on the instance with a different effective definition
(dimensions, SI scaling factor, or SI offset). Re-registering the same name with an
equivalent definition is a no-op and does not raise. Units with different names but
equivalent definitions (same composition and factor) are also not detected as
conflicts.

title: Custom Unit Systems
text:
Custom Unit Systems

A UnitSystem defines the unit used for each base dimension (mass, length,
time, and so on). In addition to the predefined systems ("SI", "CGS",
"BT"), you can define your own unit system, for example an "MMGS"
(millimeter, gram, second) system commonly used for material databases.

title: Custom Unit Systems > Custom Unit Systems From Mappings
text:
Custom Unit Systems From Mappings

Pass a base_units mapping to override only the dimensions you care about.
Unspecified dimensions default to the base system ("SI" by default):

SI-prefixed units ("mm", "km", and so on) and single-composition
derived units ("tonne", defined as 1000 kg) are accepted as long as
they are dimensionally atomic, that is, equivalent to exactly one base
dimension. Compound units that span more than one base dimension, such as
"N" or "MPa", cannot be assigned directly since pressure and force
are not base dimensions - they always emerge as derived quantities of a
consistent unit system.

A UnitSystem is only the set of base units: it has no opinion on how
derived quantities should be displayed. Choosing a display unit such as
"MPa" instead of an expanded expression is a separate concern, handled by
PreferredUnits (see below).

title: Custom Unit Systems > Preferred Units
text:
Preferred Units

For example, the classic mm-tonne-second system used by structural material
databases produces stress and pressure values that are numerically consistent
with MPa, but without any extra configuration, converting through that
system produces an expanded base-unit expression:

Pass a PreferredUnits object (or a plain string or list, which is wrapped
automatically) to Quantity.convert() to pick a named unit for matching
dimensions instead:

Because PreferredUnits is independent of the UnitSystem, the same
system produces different output depending on what is passed to
convert():

A preferred unit only applies to quantities whose dimensions match; it has no
effect on anything else, and quantities with no matching entry keep their
expanded base-unit expression.

title: Custom Unit Systems > Dimension-Only Preferred Unit Matching
text:
Dimension-Only Preferred Unit Matching

Preferred unit matching is intentionally based on dimensions only. This means
that quantities with the same dimensions use the same preferred-unit entry,
even when they represent different physical concepts. For example, torque and
energy both have dimensions M L^2 T^-2, while stress and energy density
both have dimensions M L^-1 T^-2:

Quantity-type-aware preferences are not part of PreferredUnits. If two
concepts have identical dimensions but require different display units, keep
that choice explicit in the calling code.

title: Custom Unit Systems > Registering a Named Unit System
text:
Registering a Named Unit System

Use UnitSystem.register_system() to make a fully defined custom system
reusable by name, the same way built-in systems are used. Registration only
covers the base units - keep any PreferredUnits you want to pair with it
in a separate variable:

register_system() requires every base dimension to be provided and
raises:

UnitSystemAlreadyRegistered if name is already used by a built-in
or previously registered system.

IncompleteUnitSystem if any base dimension is missing.

NotBaseUnit / IncorrectUnitType if a unit is invalid for its slot.

Registration is global for the running process, matching the behavior of the
predefined unit systems loaded from cfg.yaml.

title: Custom Unit Systems > Migrating from UnitSystem(preferred_units=...)
text:
Migrating from UnitSystem(preferred_units=...)

Earlier releases stored preferred units directly on UnitSystem. That API
has been removed because a UnitSystem (a coherent set of base units) and
a display/conversion policy (which named unit to show for a derived
quantity) are different concepts with different identities - conflating them
made equality ambiguous (two systems with identical base units but different
display choices should be substitutable, but were not). Use the table below
to migrate:





Before

After

UnitSystem(base_units=b, preferred_units=["MPa"])

UnitSystem(base_units=b) plus convert(system, preferred_units=["MPa"])

UnitSystem.register_system(name, b, preferred_units=[...])

register_system(name, b); keep a PreferredUnits alongside

us.add_preferred_units(...) / us.preferred_unit_for(d)

PreferredUnits(...) / PreferredUnits.unit_for(d)

title: Defining a quantity
text:
Defining a quantity

Import Quantity from the ansys.units package and instantiate a
Quantity object, providing a numerical value and a unit string:

You can also provide a Unit object (rather than a unit string) as a
construction argument. Alternatively, you can instantiate a Quantity
object by multiplying a Unit object by a value:

With NumPy installed, you can instantiate a Quantity using either
a list of floats or a NumPy array:

Array quantities can have any number of dimensions, including zero elements.
Indexing and slicing keep the units:

For NumPy functions such as np.sin, np.mean, or the @ operator, see
numpy_integration.

All Quantity objects work intuitively with arithmetic operators:

Additions and subtractions involving Quantity objects retain the units
of the first operand:

This formula defines the conversion of Quantity objects between different units:

value_{\text{new}} = \frac{value_{\text{si}}}{f_{\text{new}}} - c_{\text{new}}

where  is a scaling factor and  is an offset to convert
from SI units to the requested units.

To define a new unit system or create custom quantities, you can manually update the
cfg.yaml file with your desired settings. Once saved, these changes are reflected
the next time the ansys.units package is initialized.

title: Variable Descriptors
text:
Variable Descriptors

The ansys.units.variable_descriptor subpackage defines interfaces and implementations for representing physical quantities in a product-agnostic, unit-aware way. These descriptors serve as the foundation for communicating quantity metadata across Ansys systems and external APIs.

title: Variable Descriptors > Overview
text:
Overview

A VariableDescriptor encapsulates information about a physical quantity, such as:

Its name (for example, VELOCITY, FORCE)

Its associated dimensionality (via QuantityDimensions)

Optional metadata for display, categorization, or mapping to domain-specific naming schemes

These descriptors are immutable and hashable, making them suitable as keys in mappings and registries.

The subpackage also defines conversion strategies that translate between VariableDescriptor objects and external string representations (such as Fluent variable names).

A registry of predefined VariableDescriptor instances for commonly used quantities. These are typically accessed directly by name, such as VariableCatalog.``PRESSURE``.

title: Quantity Dimensions
text:
Quantity Dimensions

The ansys.units.quantity_dimensions module defines standard physical quantity dimensions, covering SI base quantities (such as mass and time) and many commonly used derived quantities (such as force, pressure, energy).

title: Quantity Dimensions > Overview
text:
Overview

A quantity dimension describes the physical nature of a value, such as length, time, or force. These dimensions are used internally in dimensional analysis, unit validation, and conversion.

This module provides a set of immutable, predefined dimension objects via the QuantityDimensions class. Each attribute of this class represents a Dimensions object composed from SI base dimensions.

These objects support symbolic operations such as multiplication, division, and exponentiation to allow for composition and comparison of dimensions.

title: Quantity Dimensions > Usage
text:
Usage

You do not create QuantityDimensions instances directly. Instead, you use the class-level attributes:

title: Quantity Dimensions > Vector Quantities
text:
Vector Quantities

Certain quantities, such as velocity or momentum, are marked as vector quantities. For these, additional attributes are automatically generated:

<NAME>_X, <NAME>_Y, <NAME>_Z - Cartesian components

<NAME>_MAGNITUDE - scalar magnitude

Example:

These variants share the same dimensional structure as the base quantity.

title: NumPy integration
text:
NumPy integration

With NumPy installed, Quantity objects work directly with NumPy functions and
universal functions. The result is a Quantity with the correct units,
and operations that don’t make sense for the units raise an error.

title: NumPy integration > Units in NumPy functions
text:
Units in NumPy functions

Functions that keep the units of their input, such as np.mean, np.max, or
np.sort, return a Quantity in the same units. Functions that combine
operands, such as np.maximum or np.concatenate, first convert all operands
to the units of the first one:

Arithmetic functions combine units in the same way as the arithmetic operators:

Plain NumPy arrays combined with quantities are treated as dimensionless:

title: NumPy integration > Trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions
text:
Trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions

np.sin, np.cos, and np.tan accept angles in any angle unit, or
dimensionless values. np.exp, np.log, and the hyperbolic functions accept
only dimensionless values. Inverse trigonometric functions return radians. Other
units raise a DimensionlessArgumentRequired error:

title: NumPy integration > Matrix multiplication
text:
Matrix multiplication

The @ operator and np.matmul multiply the units of their operands:

title: NumPy integration > Temperatures
text:
Temperatures

NumPy functions follow the same temperature rules as the arithmetic operators. See
temperature:

Absolute temperatures can’t be summed, so np.sum and np.cumsum raise a
ProhibitedTemperatureOperation error. np.mean, np.min, and np.max
are allowed.

Spreads of absolute temperatures, such as np.ptp, np.diff, and
np.std, return temperature differences.

Multiplicative functions, such as np.multiply, np.sqrt, or @, raise a
ProhibitedOffsetUnitOperation error for C and F.

title: NumPy integration > Limitations
text:
Limitations

Functions that aren’t supported, such as np.prod, raise a TypeError
instead of guessing the units of the result.

The out argument isn’t supported.

np.asarray(quantity) doesn’t remove the units. Use quantity.value to get
the plain array.

Getting started

PyAnsys Units provides a Pythonic interface for units, unit systems, and unit
conversions. Once imported the package is initialized with units and unit
systems for you to use, and is fully customizable if something you need is not
present.

classmethod register_system(name: str, base_units: Mapping[BaseDimensions, Literal['kg', 'g', 'lb', 'lbm', 'slug', 'm', 'cm', 'ft', 'inch', 'in', 's', 'A', 'mol', 'slugmol', 'cd', 'sr', 'radian', 'degree', 'rev', 'K', 'C', 'F', 'R', 'delta_K', 'delta_C', 'delta_F', 'delta_R', 'min', 'h', 'N', 'Pa', 'bar', 'W', 'J', 'V', 'farad', 'H', 'S', 'Wb', 'T', 'dyne', 'erg', 'pdl', 'psi', 'lbf', 'psf', 'ohm', 'Hz', 'l', 'gal', 'BTU', 'cal', 'coulomb', 'tonne'] | str]) -> None

Register a new named unit system for later reuse.

Once registered, the system can be created anywhere via
UnitSystem(system=name), the same way built-in systems such as
"SI", "CGS", and "BT" are used. Registration is global for
the running process (module-scoped), matching the behavior of the
predefined unit systems loaded from cfg.yaml.

Only the resolved unit name is persisted, not the Unit
object itself. Instance-scoped custom units created with
register_unit()
are not known globally by name, so while passing one here
succeeds (it is valid at registration time), reconstructing the
system later with UnitSystem(system=name) fails unless the
unit is also resolvable without that specific registry (for
example a built-in unit, or a prefixed/derived atomic unit).

Parameters

name: str

Name of the new unit system, for example "MMGS".

base_units: dict

Units mapped to base dimensions types. Every member of
BaseDimensions must be
provided so the resulting system is fully defined.

Raises

UnitSystemAlreadyRegistered

If name is already used by a built-in or previously
registered unit system.

IncompleteUnitSystem

If base_units is missing one or more base dimensions.

NotBaseUnit

If a unit is not dimensionally atomic (for example a derived
unit that spans more than one base dimension, such as "Pa").

IncorrectUnitType

If a unit does not match its intended base dimension.

Examples

Register a custom “mm, g, s” (MMGS) unit system:

>>> from ansys.units import BaseDimensions, UnitSystem
>>> dims = BaseDimensions
>>> UnitSystem.register_system(
...     name="MMGS",
...     base_units={
...         dims.MASS: "g",
...         dims.LENGTH: "mm",
...         dims.TIME: "s",
...         dims.TEMPERATURE: "K",
...         dims.TEMPERATURE_DIFFERENCE: "delta_K",
...         dims.ANGLE: "radian",
...         dims.CHEMICAL_AMOUNT: "mol",
...         dims.LIGHT: "cd",
...         dims.CURRENT: "A",
...         dims.SOLID_ANGLE: "sr",
...     },
... )
>>> mmgs = UnitSystem(system="MMGS")

classmethod register_system(name: str, base_units: Mapping[BaseDimensions, Literal['kg', 'g', 'lb', 'lbm', 'slug', 'm', 'cm', 'ft', 'inch', 'in', 's', 'A', 'mol', 'slugmol', 'cd', 'sr', 'radian', 'degree', 'rev', 'K', 'C', 'F', 'R', 'delta_K', 'delta_C', 'delta_F', 'delta_R', 'min', 'h', 'N', 'Pa', 'bar', 'W', 'J', 'V', 'farad', 'H', 'S', 'Wb', 'T', 'dyne', 'erg', 'pdl', 'psi', 'lbf', 'psf', 'ohm', 'Hz', 'l', 'gal', 'BTU', 'cal', 'coulomb', 'tonne'] | str]) -> None

Register a new named unit system for later reuse.

Once registered, the system can be created anywhere via
UnitSystem(system=name), the same way built-in systems such as
"SI", "CGS", and "BT" are used. Registration is global for
the running process (module-scoped), matching the behavior of the
predefined unit systems loaded from cfg.yaml.

Only the resolved unit name is persisted, not the Unit
object itself. Instance-scoped custom units created with
register_unit()
are not known globally by name, so while passing one here
succeeds (it is valid at registration time), reconstructing the
system later with UnitSystem(system=name) fails unless the
unit is also resolvable without that specific registry (for
example a built-in unit, or a prefixed/derived atomic unit).

Parameters

name: str

Name of the new unit system, for example "MMGS".

base_units: dict

Units mapped to base dimensions types. Every member of
BaseDimensions must be
provided so the resulting system is fully defined.

Raises

UnitSystemAlreadyRegistered

If name is already used by a built-in or previously
registered unit system.

IncompleteUnitSystem

If base_units is missing one or more base dimensions.

NotBaseUnit

If a unit is not dimensionally atomic (for example a derived
unit that spans more than one base dimension, such as "Pa").

IncorrectUnitType

If a unit does not match its intended base dimension.

Examples

Register a custom “mm, g, s” (MMGS) unit system:

>>> from ansys.units import BaseDimensions, UnitSystem
>>> dims = BaseDimensions
>>> UnitSystem.register_system(
...     name="MMGS",
...     base_units={
...         dims.MASS: "g",
...         dims.LENGTH: "mm",
...         dims.TIME: "s",
...         dims.TEMPERATURE: "K",
...         dims.TEMPERATURE_DIFFERENCE: "delta_K",
...         dims.ANGLE: "radian",
...         dims.CHEMICAL_AMOUNT: "mol",
...         dims.LIGHT: "cd",
...         dims.CURRENT: "A",
...         dims.SOLID_ANGLE: "sr",
...     },
... )
>>> mmgs = UnitSystem(system="MMGS")
>>> mmgs.LENGTH
'mm'

title: Temperature and temperature difference
text:
Temperature and temperature difference

PyAnsys Units supports temperature units in kelvin (K), celsius (C), rankine (R)
and fahrenheit (F).

For each temperature unit, there is a corresponding temperature difference unit
which is prefixed with delta_. To add two temperature-based quantities,
at least one must be a temperature difference. If one temperature is subtracted
from another, the result is a temperature difference.

Any temperature values below absolute zero are instantiated as temperature
difference. For arrays, the lowest value decides.

The lower limit comes from each unit’s conversion offset rather than its name, so
it also applies to custom temperature units. You can query it directly:

title: Temperature and temperature difference > Offset units
text:
Offset units

The celsius (C) and fahrenheit (F) units are offset units: their zero point
differs from absolute zero, so scaling a value in these units has no physical
meaning. Kelvin (K), rankine (R), and all temperature difference units are
multiplicative.

Multiplying, dividing, or raising an absolute temperature in C or F to a power
raises a ProhibitedOffsetUnitOperation error. Convert to K or R, or use a
temperature difference, instead:

Unit("C").has_offset reports whether a unit is an offset unit.

Offset units inside compound units, such as W m^-1 C^-1, are interpreted as
temperature differences. These compound units convert without an offset and
support all arithmetic. If unit arithmetic cancels such a compound unit down to a
single temperature term, the result is a temperature difference unit:

Multiplier prefixes, such as kC or mF, can’t be combined with offset units
and raise a PrefixedOffsetUnit error.

title: Angles
text:
Angles

PyAnsys Units treats angles as non-dimensional unit quantity by default but it
supports configuration of angle quantities as dimension.
Angle quantity units such as degree, radian and solid angle can be treated as dimension.

You can set the environment variable PYANSYS_UNITS_ANGLE_AS_DIMENSION to treat angle quantity
units as dimension.

title: PyAnsys Units documentation 0.16.0 > Overview
text:
Overview

PyAnsys Units provides a Pythonic interface for units, unit systems, and unit
conversions. Its features enable seamless setup and usage of physical
quantities, enabling you to perform these tasks:

Instantiate physical quantities from a unit string, list of dimensions, or
quantity table.

Perform unit conversions and arithmetic operations between quantity objects or
real values.

Create custom units and unit systems.

Documentation for the latest stable release of PyAnsys Units is hosted at PyAnsys Units documentation.

the documentation for the development version or previously released versions.

On the PyAnsys Units Issues page, you can
create issues to report bugs, and request new features. On the PyAnsys Units Discussions page or the Discussions
page on the Ansys Developer portal, you can post questions, share ideas, and get community feedback.

To reach the project support team, email pyansys.core@ansys.com.

Bases: object

An immutable mapping from dimensions to a preferred unit name.

PreferredUnits is a conversion policy: it decides which named derived unit,
such as "MPa", is emitted instead of an expanded base-unit expression, such as
"tonne mm^-1 s^-2", when a quantity is converted through a
UnitSystem. It is independent of any particular
UnitSystem and is passed directly to
convert().

Entries are matched only by dimensions. Quantities with the same dimensions,
such as torque and energy (both M L^2 T^-2), or stress and energy density
(both M L^-1 T^-2), share the same preferred-unit entry.

Parameters

units: optional

Preferred unit entries: a single unit name, a Unit
instance, any object with a name, or a sequence of these values.

Raises

UnconfiguredPreferredUnit

If a unit cannot be resolved to a known, dimensioned unit.

PreferredUnitAlreadyRegistered

If two entries would register different units for the same dimensions.

Examples

>>> from ansys.units import PreferredUnits
>>> prefs = PreferredUnits(["MPa", "N"])

Return the preferred unit name for dimensions, if one is configured.

title: Serialization
text:
Serialization

PyAnsys Units can save quantities and units to dictionaries, JSON, strings, and
pickle files, and restore them.

title: Serialization > Dictionaries
text:
Dictionaries

to_dict() returns built-in Python types only. Array values become nested lists,
and extra fields given to the Quantity constructor are kept:

title: Serialization > JSON
text:
JSON

Quantity works as a field in Pydantic models,
which use the same dictionary format:

Without Pydantic, use the json module with to_dict() and from_dict():

title: Serialization > Strings
text:
Strings

Quantity.from_string() parses the output of str(quantity):

NumPy shortens the string of large arrays with .... Such strings can’t be
parsed, so use to_dict() for large arrays.

title: Serialization > Pickle
text:
Pickle

Units are pickled by name and resolved again when loaded from a pickle. Pickle
files created with earlier versions of PyAnsys Units can still be loaded.

title: Serialization > Custom units
text:
Custom units

Units are stored by name. Custom units registered with
UnitRegistry.register_unit() are also stored with their
definition, so they can be restored without the registry:

When loading, a unit name is looked up in this order:

The registry argument of from_dict() or from_string().

The registry set with set_application_registry(). Loading from a pickle
also uses this registry.

The built-in units.

If the stored definition of a custom unit differs from the unit with the same name
in the registry, loading raises a ConflictingUnitDefinition error rather than
returning wrong values. A unit name that can’t be resolved raises an
UnresolvableUnit error.

title: Frequently asked questions
text: Frequently asked questions

title: Frequently asked questions > What is PyAnsys Units?
text:
What is PyAnsys Units?

PyAnsys units is a Python package that allows you to introduce the concept of
physical quantities into your Python environment. You can define your own units,
unit systems and quantities and work with them in a natural way using arithmetic
operations and conversions.

title: Frequently asked questions > What unit systems are provided by default?
text:
What unit systems are provided by default?

PyAnsys Units provides the following unit systems by default:

International System of Units (SI)

Centimetre gram second (CGS)

British Technical (BT)

British technical units define the mass units as the slug, length units as
ft and time units of s, which leads to pound-force, lbf, being the
force units. You can introduce your own unit systems either dynamically at run
time or by providing a custom configuration file.

PyAnsys Units defines a unit system as a unique selection of base units. For
instance, the SI unit system is a unique choice of units for the default base
units.

title: Frequently asked questions > How is PyAnsys Units different from pint?
text:
How is PyAnsys Units different from pint?

In contrast to pint, the UnitRegistry is only a container of the configured
Unit objects. The registry does not contain additional information. Notably
the UnitSystem is a standalone class. When creating a Unit using
Dimensions it requires a unit system parameter to be passed in for non-SI
units.

Equivalent units are also handled differently. Any two Unit objects that
have the same dimensions, SI offset, and SI scaling factor are evaluated as
equal.

PyAnsys Units treats all angles as dimensional units. With this behavior the
conversion from rad/s to Hz is not allowed.

title: Registering Custom Units
text:
Registering Custom Units

You can register new derived units at runtime using instance-scoped
registration on a UnitRegistry instance.

title: Registering Custom Units > At Construction
text:
At Construction

Use the custom_units parameter to register units when creating a registry.
Each entry supports an optional "aliases" list:

title: Registering Custom Units > After Construction
text:
After Construction

Use register_unit() to add units to an existing registry. Two equivalent
calling conventions are supported: a composition/factor form, and an
object-based form that accepts a Unit or Quantity definition. Both
forms accept an optional aliases argument:

The object-based form accepts a Quantity (as produced by factor * unit)
or a bare Unit (treated as a factor of 1).

title: Registering Custom Units > String-Based Lookup
text:
String-Based Lookup

Registered units, and their aliases, can be accessed by name using:

ur.get_unit(name) - Returns the Unit object

ur.Quantity(value, name) - Creates a Quantity with the registered unit

The global Quantity() constructor does not see instance-registered units.
Use ur.Quantity() for string-based creation with custom units.

title: Registering Custom Units > Instance Isolation
text:
Instance Isolation

Each registry maintains its own set of registered units:

title: Registering Custom Units > Collision Detection
text:
Collision Detection

Built-in unit names (m, kg, J, etc.) can never be overridden,
even with an equivalent definition.

Re-registering an existing custom name with the same effective
definition (dimensions, SI scaling factor, and SI offset) is a no-op:
it returns the existing unit instead of raising. This makes repeated setup
calls idempotent.

Re-registering an existing custom name with a different effective
definition raises UnitNameAlreadyRegistered.

Equivalent definitions registered under different names are still
allowed (the check only applies to the exact name being registered).

title: Registering Custom Units > Notes
text:
Notes

composition must be a valid unit string composed of configured base/derived
units (for example, "N m").

factor is the scale factor relating the composition to the new unit symbol.

aliases additional names resolve to the same registered Unit object
and are subject to the same collision rules as the primary name.

title: Registering Custom Units > Persistence
text:
Persistence

Custom units registered at runtime are not written back to cfg.yaml
or any installed configuration file. They only live on the UnitRegistry
instance and are lost once that instance (or the process) goes away.

To persist custom units across sessions, export them to your own YAML file
and reload them explicitly. This only exports units added via
register_unit() (including through custom_units/custom_units_file);
built-in units are never included:

export_custom_units() raises ValueError if the registry has no
custom units to export, and raises FileExistsError if the destination
file already exists (pass overwrite=True to replace it).

This export/import mechanism is independent of register_alias(),
whose global aliases are never persisted (see unit_aliases).

title: Dimensions
text:
Dimensions



class ansys.units.dimensions.Dimensions(dimensions: Mapping[BaseDimensions, float] | None = None, copy_from: Dimensions | None = None)

Bases: object

A representation of an arbitrary number of dimensions, where each dimension is a
pair consisting of a base dimension and exponent.

A dictionary of BaseDimensions and exponent is required
for a non-dimensionless object.

If any keys are duplicated in copy_from and dimensions then the
associated values from dimensions are used.

Parameters

title: Serialization
text:
Serialization



Serialization of Unit and Quantity objects.

Supported formats:

Plain dictionaries: Quantity.to_dict() and Quantity.from_dict()
(and the Unit equivalents). This is also the format used by the pydantic
integration, which provides JSON support (model_dump_json,
TypeAdapter(Quantity).dump_json). Without pydantic, use
json.dumps(quantity.to_dict()) and
Quantity.from_dict(json.loads(text)).

Strings: Quantity.from_string() parses the output of str(quantity).

Pickle: units are pickled by name and resolved again when unpickled.

Units are always stored by name. When loading, a name is resolved against an
explicitly given UnitRegistry, then against the
application registry (see set_application_registry()), and finally
against the built-in units. Custom units that are only known to a registry are
stored together with their definition so that they can be restored even when
no registry defines them.



ansys.units.serialization.set_application_registry(registry: UnitRegistry | None) -> None

Set the registry used to resolve unit names when loading serialized data.

The application registry is used by unpickling and by any loading function
called without an explicit registry. This
allows custom units registered with
register_unit() to be restored by name.

Parameters

registry

UnitRegistry or python:None

Registry to use, or None to use only the built-in units.

Examples

>>> import pickle
>>> from ansys.units import UnitRegistry, set_application_registry
>>> ur = UnitRegistry()
>>> micron = ur.register_unit(unit="micron", composition="m", factor=1e-6)
>>> set_application_registry(ur)
>>> q = pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(ur.Quantity(3, "micron")))
>>> q.units == ur.micron
True



ansys.units.serialization.get_application_registry() -> UnitRegistry | None

Return the registry set with set_application_registry(), if any.

title: Pandas Integration for ansys-units > Cumulative Operations and Unique Values
text:
Cumulative Operations and Unique Values

A cumulative product of quantities would have different units for each value, so
cumprod() is only available for dimensionless series:

title: Pandas Integration for ansys-units > Rolling, Expanding, and Exponentially Weighted Windows
text:
Rolling, Expanding, and Exponentially Weighted Windows

pandas converts window data to plain floats, so series.rolling(2).mean() has no
units. Use the .units accessor to keep them:

sum, mean, median, min, max, quantile, first, and last
keep the units of the series. std and sem are in the units of a difference,
and var is in squared units. Results whose units can’t be determined, such as
count, apply, and corr, are plain floats.

title: Pandas Integration for ansys-units > Grouping
text:
Grouping

Grouped aggregations keep the units of the column:

Grouped prod() and cumprod() are only available for dimensionless columns,
because each group would otherwise have different units.

title: Pandas Integration for ansys-units > Temperatures
text:
Temperatures

Unit-aware series follow the same temperature rules as quantities. See
temperature:

Absolute temperatures, such as quantity[C], can’t be summed, so sum() and
cumsum() raise a ProhibitedTemperatureOperation error, including in grouped
aggregations. mean(), min(), and max() are allowed.

The standard deviation and variance of absolute temperatures are temperature
differences, for example delta_C and delta_C^2.

title: Pandas Integration for ansys-units > Limitations
text:
Limitations

Products: cumprod() and grouped prod() raise a TypeError unless the
series is dimensionless, because each result would have different units.

Built-in windows and describe(): series.rolling(), series.expanding(),
series.ewm(), and series.describe() return plain floats. Use the .units
versions of these methods to keep units.

Preferred units as a conversion policy

PreferredUnits is a separate conversion policy object, independent of
UnitSystem, that you pass explicitly to convert(). A UnitSystem
only defines base units, so converting through it produces an expanded
base-unit expression unless a PreferredUnits policy is supplied.
